summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women throughout Eswatini as of 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition exists, so a trans visitor's passport and other documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender. A trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law, and there is no registered advocacy body in the country to turn to for help.

LGBTI organisations cannot obtain registration. The registrar of companies refused to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities in June 2019 on grounds of morality. In April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. The gap between the constitutional finding and the registration outcome leaves no licensed national organisation able to represent or assist a visitor.

Hostility from public figures is on the record. In 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said people of the same sex cannot even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position. Former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law in 2012 on the grounds that so few gay people lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort. A 2021 United States State Department report recorded traditional, religious and government officials describing same-sex conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The wider political setting is an absolute monarchy rated Not Free by Freedom House in its 2024 report, with an overall score of 17 out of 100 (1 out of 40 for political rights, 16 out of 60 for civil liberties) and severely restricted civic space. The BTI 2024 country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups inside a broader pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment.

No same-sex relationship is legally recognised, and no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity apply in education, health, housing or employment.

Health settings are a documented point of exposure. A 2019 survey found that 59 per cent of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30 per cent had been denied healthcare services. Policy points the other way in places: section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and the 2021 National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence and define gender-based violence to include violence based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity.

Violence against people perceived as gender or sexual minorities is documented. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. Rock of Hope reports that, with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most choose to remain closeted or move to South Africa.
tangentialFactors:
Public visibility has occurred without recorded incident. The first eSwatini Pride, held in July 2018, was declared a success, and a virtual Pride celebration in June 2021 passed without incident according to the 2021 State Department report. A church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018, documented alongside continuing discrimination in the kingdom.

Several policy instruments reference sexual orientation without creating enforceable rights. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles, the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as freedom from discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, and the 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed.
localsOnly:
Residents face the consequences of the registration block directly: with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, Rock of Hope reports that LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most remain closeted or move to South Africa.

A 2013 survey found that 43 per cent of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78 per cent regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal.

Family law treats same-sex couples differently from heterosexual ones. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced, and no same-sex relationship is legally recognised.
outOfScopeNotes:
The statutory provision that criminalises same-sex conduct in Eswatini, the penalty it carries, and any recorded prosecution or conviction are not sourced. Enforcement practice against visitors is therefore unresolved.

Police or immigration treatment of trans travellers specifically is not documented, and no trans-specific violent incident with a recorded outcome is available. Whether the April 2022 High Court ruling was appealed, and whether the registration refusal has been revisited since, is not established.

Violence figures available are individual incidents and survey responses rather than a measured rate, and no comparison with the general homicide rate is available.
